**Audit: 1860 Census Record (`ark:/61903/1:1:MABC`)**

The record has three extracted assertions, all on the `child_2` persona (Patrick Flynn, age 15):

| Assertion | Type | Linked? | pe_ entry |
|-----------|------|---------|-----------|
| a_008 | name: "Patrick Flynn" | No | — |
| a_009 | birth: "age 15, Ireland" | No | — |
| a_010 | relationship: household position as son of Thomas Flynn | Partial — one side only | pe_004 (→ I1 only) |

---

**Three gaps identified:**

**Gap 1 — a_008 and a_009 are unlinked.**
The name and birth assertions for the `child_2` persona carry no `person_evidence` entry at all. They should also point to I1 (Patrick Flynn), since they are the primary identity anchors — the name match and age-derived birth year are what actually ground the identification.

**Gap 2 — a_010 is not linked to I2 (Thomas Flynn) on the head-of-household side.**
A relationship assertion bears on both parties. pe_004 links a_010 to I1 (Patrick), but there is no corresponding `pe_` entry linking a_010 to I2 (Thomas Flynn). Both-sided pe_ entries are required for relationship-implying assertions.

**Gap 3 — pe_004's confidence and match score have concerns.**
The existing link is recorded as `confident` with a null `match_score`. Since I1 was not minted from this persona, `same_person` should have been called and its score recorded. The rationale is also thin — no date-check or residence-check, no score reference — and `confident` may be too strong for a link grounded only in an inferred household-position relationship.

---

**Recommended actions:**
1. Create pe_ entries linking **a_008** and **a_009** to I1.
2. Create a pe_ entry linking **a_010** to **I2** (Thomas Flynn).
3. Call `same_person` for the a_010 → I1 pairing, capture the match score in pe_004, and reconsider whether `confident` is the right tier.

Would you like me to proceed with any or all of these corrective actions?

The name and birth assertions for the `child_2` persona carry no `person_evidence` entry at all. They belong to the same persona as a_010, so they should also point to I1 (Patrick Flynn). These two assertions are the primary identity anchors — the name match and the age-derived birth year are what actually ground the link — yet neither is linked. pe_004 rests only on the relationship assertion, which is the weakest of the three (it is inferred from household position, not directly stated).

**Gap 2 — a_010 is not linked to I2 (Thomas Flynn) on the head-of-household side.**
A relationship assertion bears on both parties. a_010 names Thomas Flynn as head of household and places Patrick in his household as a child-inferred relative. pe_004 links a_010 to I1 (the child), but there is no corresponding `pe_` entry linking a_010 to I2 (Thomas Flynn). Per the cardinality rule, both-sided pe_ entries are mandatory for every relationship-implying assertion. The Thomas Flynn side is missing.

**Gap 3 — pe_004's confidence and rationale have concerns.**
The existing link (a_010 → I1) is recorded as `confident` with a null `match_score`. I1 is an existing tree person whose source refs point to the 1850 census and the death certificate — not to this 1860 record — so I1 was not minted from the persona being linked here. review_dimensions.name: Confidence calibration
review_dimensions.rationale: All four family members received 'confident' links, which is appropriate. The head-of-household persona (I1) has multiple independent corroborating sources (1860 and 1880 censuses), exact name match, birth year match (b. ~1822), and household head position consistency. The move from England to Utah is bridged by the documented LDS emigration corridor from the FamilySearch wiki, which explains the geographic gap. The rationales explicitly cite the corridor ('Many Latter-day Saint immigrants leaving Europe and Great Britain came on chartered ships from Liverpool, England'). Household members (I2, I3, I4) are linked with 'confident' based on household position, name matches, and age consistency across the two censuses. No chronological contradictions exist; ages progress consistently (e.g., Joseph Jr. age 10 in 1860 → age 30 in 1880, a 20-year gap). The confidence tier matches the identity-evidence strength.

review_dimensions.name: Rationale quality
review_dimensions.rationale: Each rationale cites multiple specific matching attributes: name (exact match), age/birth year (consistent with tree), household position (head, wife, son, daughter), and location (Salt Lake County, Utah Territory). Rationales address the geographic move explicitly by naming the distance (7,767 km) and the corridor that bridges it. For example, pe_001 states: 'Name Joseph Pratt exact match; head of household, Salt Lake County. Score 0.78 (strong). Strong match on name, birth year, and household head position; corridor bridges the England-to-Utah move.' Rationales distinguish between different assertion types (name, birth, residence, relationship) and explain why each supports the link. Competing candidates are implicitly ruled out by the strong household correlation and name-age-location alignment.

review_dimensions.name: Multi-person awareness
review_dimensions.rationale: Relationship assertions in the 1880 census (a_017: wife of Joseph; a_018: son of Joseph) were linked to both parties. Assertion a_017 generated two person_evidence entries: pe_015 (I2 as wife) and pe_016 (I1 as husband named in the relationship). Assertion a_018 generated two entries: pe_019 (I4 as son) and pe_020 (I1 as father named in the relationship). Both sides of each relationship are represented in the person_evidence links, satisfying the cardinality requirement.

review_dimensions.name: Person minting and connecting edges
review_dimensions.rationale: No new persons needed to be minted; all four family members (I1, I2, I3, I4) already existed in the tree. The skill correctly linked assertions to existing persons via person_evidence entries. Materialize_facts was called for all seven person-record combinations (I1, I2, I3, I4 for 1860; I1, I2, I4 for 1880), enriching existing persons with sourced facts and references. No edges needed to be written because these are non-household records (census records are household records, but the skill correctly enriched facts rather than creating new persons). The materialize_facts results show facts were added (e.g., I1 gained 2 Residence facts for 1860 and 1880) and names/facts were enriched with source references. No merge_warnings dry-run was needed because no new persons were being created. Confidence is calibrated appropriately (confident for I1 with multiple sources; confident for household members based on position and correlation).

review_dimensions.name: Score discipline
review_dimensions.rationale: same_person was called for all 12 relevant assertion-person pairings: a_001, a_002, a_009 (I1 from 1860); a_003, a_004 (I2 from 1860); a_005, a_006 (I3 from 1860); a_007, a_008 (I4 from 1860); a_010, a_011, a_016 (I1 from 1880); a_012, a_013 (I2 from 1880); a_014, a_015, a_018 (I4 from 1880); plus a_017 and a_018 scored against I1 with recordRole='head' for the relationship assertions. All calls returned score 0.78 (high confidence match). The score informed but did not dictate the confidence tier; the rationales cite the score as supporting evidence ('Score 0.78 (strong)') but ground the confident link in the correlation analysis (name, age, household position, corridor). recordRole was correctly omitted for the assertion's own party and supplied only for the second party in relationship assertions (a_017, a_018 scored against head with recordRole='head'). match_score is recorded in all person_evidence entries and properly reflects the same_person results.

The 1860 Berks County census linked two children to George Ackerman's household: Henry, probably born around 1851, and Margaret, probably born around 1854, both in Pennsylvania. agent_returns.text:
All five persons clear — no warnings.

**Links created:**
- pe_001–pe_003: 1870 census head (William Weller, CP1) → I1 — `probable`
- pe_004–pe_005: 1870 census household_member_1 (Mary Weller, CP2) → I2 — `probable`
- pe_006–pe_007: 1870 census household_member_2 (James Weller, CP3) → I3 — `probable`
- pe_008–pe_009: 1870 census household_member_3 (Ellen Weller, CP4) → I4 — `probable`
- pe_010–pe_011: 1870 census household_member_4 (George Weller, CP5) → I5 — `probable`
- pe_012–pe_014: 1880 census head (William Weller, DP1) → I1 — `probable`
- pe_015–pe_017: 1880 census wife (Mary Weller, DP2) → I2 — `probable` (including the relationship assertion bearing on both I2 and I1)
- pe_018: 1880 relationship assertion bearing on I1 as named husband — `probable`
- pe_019–pe_021: 1880 census son (George Weller, DP3) → I5 — `probable` (including relationship bearing on I5 and I1)
- pe_022: 1880 relationship assertion bearing on I1 as named father — `probable`

**Why `probable` and not `confident`:** The records place the family in Maury County, Tennessee; the tree attests William's birthplace in Horsham, Sussex, England — a move of 6,804 km. The Tennessee Emigration and Immigration wiki page notes that "most of the overseas immigrants preferred the industrialized North rather than the agricultural South," and names no England-to-Tennessee corridor for the 1860s era. No passenger list, naturalization record, or other documentary bridge for the move is in the project. An unexplained international move caps all links at `probable`.

**Edges:** All parent-child and couple edges already exist in the tree; no new edges needed.

**Household absence flag (1880):** James Weller (I3) and Ellen Weller (I4) appear in the 1870 census but not in 1880. Neither has a recorded death. Possibilities: both had moved out and established separate households by 1880 (James would be ~28, Ellen ~25 — plausible ages for independent living), or either or both died before 1880, or they were enumerated elsewhere. This warrants further research before those two persons can be called absent rather than missing.

---

Both census records have been matched to the family in the tree. The 1870 record shows all five Wellers together — William as head, his wife Mary, and three children James, Ellen, and George — and the 1880 record shows William and Mary still in Maury County, Tennessee, with only their youngest son George still at home. All eight matches are rated "probably" rather than "very likely" because the family originated in Horsham, Sussex, England and nothing on file explains how or when they crossed to Tennessee; finding a passenger list or naturalization record for William would likely lift all the links to the highest confidence level.

To move forward, the best next step is to search for a passenger list or naturalization record that bridges the Wellers' move from England to Tennessee, and separately to look for James and Ellen Weller in the 1880 census to find out where they were living by then.
